title: Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data

concept.text: The innovation would make broadly programmable computation on encrypted data affordable for ordinary applications. A server could process ciphertexts and return an encrypted result without receiving the secret key needed to read the underlying data. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) already provides the cryptographic basis for this capability; the proposed breakthrough is reducing its time and memory costs to a small factor of comparable plaintext computation.

Generality matters: the target extends beyond shallow statistics, a single optimized model inference, or a special protocol for one function. FHE supports computation of arbitrary circuit depth in principle, subject to finite computational resources. This does not mean that every program currently runs efficiently, or that any physical computation can continue indefinitely.

Concept definition: routine cost means that encryption overhead becomes small enough to fit ordinary application budgets across a broad range of workloads. The proposed factor-of-10 benchmark below is one possible operational test of that goal. Neither that numerical threshold nor any particular accelerator architecture defines the innovation.

significance.text: The direct consequence would be a much broader practical ability to outsource confidential computation. The supplied survey describes both computation on ciphertexts and substantial computational and storage overhead. If that overhead fell to a small factor of plaintext costs, many more applications could process sensitive inputs on machines that are not entrusted with the decryption key. The revolutionary change would be making an existing cryptographic capability economical across ordinary workloads.

Conditional application synthesis: this could expand confidential cloud analytics, collaboration over sensitive medical data, and other services that need useful results without exposing their underlying inputs to the computing provider. Hospitals or election offices are possible beneficiaries, but the supplied evidence does not establish their present deployment practices or show that economical FHE alone would satisfy their operational requirements. Adoption would still depend on application design, key management, integration, and an appropriate security model.

Security interpretation from the supplied review: encrypted computation alone does not guarantee that a malicious server executed the requested computation correctly, prevent sensitive information from being revealed by authorized outputs, or establish program privacy. Those properties require additional mechanisms or assumptions. Consequently, routine-cost FHE would be a major enabling technology rather than a complete guarantee of confidential and trustworthy application behavior.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a broadly programmable encrypted-computation system whose complete resource costs ordinary applications can afford. The March 2024 survey documents a historical gap between that goal and existing implementations. Its coverage of research from 2019–2022 supports the technical challenge, but does not establish whether the gap remains open as of November 1, 2026.

The documented barriers include expensive polynomial arithmetic, key-switching, bootstrapping, and memory movement. Key-switching transforms ciphertext representations during evaluation, while bootstrapping refreshes ciphertexts so computation can continue despite accumulated noise. These operations impose substantial computational and storage demands. Memory bandwidth and management also matter: accelerating arithmetic alone does not establish that the whole application has become economical.

The survey also identifies the need for general acceleration frameworks that meet differing application requirements, security-sensitive parameter selection, and better comparison baselines. The engineering challenge therefore includes making performance portable across workloads while retaining explicit security and numerical-accuracy targets. The evidence documents costly operations and unresolved design problems; it does not establish a lower bound proving that large overhead is unavoidable.

current_state.text: FHE exists and has software implementations. The verified survey attributes the first FHE scheme to Craig Gentry in 2009 and describes subsequent implementation libraries and acceleration approaches. The separately supplied citation to Gentry’s STOC paper has no captured document in the source index, so this account relies on the survey rather than an independent inspection of the original construction or abstract.

Gong and colleagues’ survey, published March 1, 2024, examines research conducted from 2019 through 2022. It describes substantial computational and storage overhead, identifies bootstrapping as a major time and space bottleneck, and discusses polynomial arithmetic, key-switching, memory bandwidth, and implementation flexibility. Its assessment is that hardware acceleration is bringing FHE closer to practice, while theoretical improvements may take considerable time. These are dated assessments, not demonstrations of routine-cost general computation.

The earlier research attributes to the 2024 ACM survey “SoK: Fully Homomorphic Encryption Accelerators” an assessment that FHE computation remains orders of magnitude slower than plaintext and that bootstrapping can dominate runtime. That ACM document was not captured in the supplied source index, so the review could not verify those specific attributions. They remain reported historical claims rather than independently established quantitative findings in this record.

The earlier research also reports that IACR ePrint 2025/686 bootstraps 2-bit through 8-bit messages in 1.46 ms through 28.5 ms, respectively, and associates the result with October 2025. No captured ePrint text is available in the supplied evidence, so the date, timings, experimental conditions, and publication status beyond the ePrint designation remain unverified. Even if confirmed, these would be measurements of a cryptographic primitive on small messages; they would not by themselves establish comparable overhead for complete general programs.

Evidence boundary: according to the supplied review, the March 2024 survey was available as a complete 23-page PDF text extraction and an HTML article body. Figures were not inspected, and table and figure contents were incompletely represented in HTML; the findings retained here do not depend on those visual elements. The supplied freshness record is empty. Consequently, this record cannot establish the frontier of encrypted computation as of November 1, 2026, or claim that no qualifying result appeared in 2026. Missing captured evidence does not show that the reported ACM or ePrint findings are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: publish a reproducible suite combining database queries, cryptographic operations, and model inference. Specify dataset sizes, query types, cryptographic workloads, and the model’s architecture, size, and numerical precision at evaluation time. Run the suite through a broadly programmable FHE implementation; a specialized protocol for one function, such as private set intersection, would not meet this proposed breadth requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Broadly programmable FHE runs specified query, cryptographic, and inference workloads

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance threshold: require end-to-end elapsed time and peak memory each to remain within 10 times the corresponding plaintext baseline on the same machine, with matched outputs or explicitly declared numerical accuracy. Publish both implementations and their hardware and software configurations so the baseline is meaningful. The factor of 10 is a proposed criterion, not an established community standard or an achieved result.
completion_criteria.label: Same-machine end-to-end time and peak memory within 10× plaintext

completion_criteria.text: Proposed security and accounting requirements: state the lattice assumption, security target, cryptographic parameters, and threat model. Report setup, key generation, encryption, evaluation, decryption, and data-transfer costs, together with key and ciphertext sizes. Identify which costs are amortized and over how many operations or users, and disclose workload-specific preprocessing and client participation. These requirements are intended to make the practical cost claim auditable.
completion_criteria.label: Stated security basis with full amortized resource costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements: independent teams should reproduce the results using public code, inputs or reproducible input generators, and complete parameters. Report performance as workload size and computational depth increase, including cases that exceed the proposed cost threshold. Passing a finite suite would establish demonstrated breadth on those workloads, not a universal overhead bound for every program. Claims about malicious-server correctness, program privacy, or protection from output disclosure would need separate demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction including above-threshold cases and stated limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction — CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation: both concepts concern cryptographic control over computation. CSC-05 focuses on processing encrypted inputs economically; CSC-09 concerns an obfuscation capability associated with concealing program information. Routine-cost encrypted computation should not be treated as achieving indistinguishability obfuscation. The supplied material does not establish the precise formal relationship or implementation boundary between them.

Roster-based distinction — CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems: a sufficiently broad collapse of computational hardness could have major consequences for cryptography. However, the earlier categorical assertion that a feasible NP-complete algorithm would remove the assumptions used by these schemes is not established by the supplied evidence. Assessing that connection requires precise algorithmic costs, the particular FHE assumption, and the security parameters. CSC-05 seeks economical encrypted computation under explicit security assumptions.

Roster-based distinction — CSC-02, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation: both concern making demanding computational capabilities practical, but quantum-computing capability is not itself a demonstration of low-overhead encrypted computation. Any security interaction would need analysis of the particular cryptographic assumptions; the supplied evidence establishes no specific reduction or dependence between these entries.

Roster-based distinction — CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software, and CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models: these address forms of assurance about software or model behavior. They could complement confidential computation, but neither should be conflated with FHE privacy. A fast encrypted computation does not by itself prove correct execution or establish the behavioral guarantees of the program being evaluated.

Conditional roster synthesis — CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence; CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems; CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery; and CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments: economical FHE could potentially protect sensitive inputs to computational components of these systems. It would not itself supply intelligence, explain generalization, produce reliable mathematical discoveries, or deliver physical autonomy. These are possible application connections rather than demonstrated dependencies.

unresolved_issues: Whether routine-cost broadly programmable encrypted computation remained unachieved on November 1, 2026 cannot be determined from the supplied evidence.
The ACM survey’s exact slowdown assessment and bootstrapping-runtime attribution remain unverified because no captured document was supplied.
The ePrint’s reported timings, October 2025 date, hardware, parameters, security target, batching conditions, and subsequent peer-review status remain unverified.
The original Gentry paper was not captured; its construction and abstract were not independently verified in the supplied review.
The factor-of-10 threshold remains a proposal. Its suitability across application budgets, workload scales, accuracy requirements, and amortization regimes requires further justification.
The precise formal relationship with CSC-09 and the consequences of any particular practical NP-complete algorithm for the chosen FHE assumptions remain unresolved.

The review recommended removing unverified numerical and attribution claims from the factual current-state account. They are instead retained as explicitly unverified reports because the task requests preservation of useful quantitative detail and uncertainty; no missing evidence has been treated as resolved.

brief.title: Affordable computing that keeps data encrypted
possible: You could let a cloud service work on confidential data without giving it the key to read that data. It would return an encrypted answer, at a time and memory cost ordinary applications could afford.
The capability would cover a broad range of programs, from database queries to running trained models, rather than a specially optimized task.
why: More organisations could outsource useful work on sensitive information while keeping the computing provider from reading the inputs. This could expand confidential cloud analysis and collaboration over medical data.

shown: Fully homomorphic encryption, which lets servers calculate with encrypted data without the secret key, already has working software. Gong and colleagues surveyed acceleration methods and found substantial computing and storage costs.
One major bottleneck is bootstrapping: refreshing encrypted data so calculations can continue despite accumulated noise. Faster arithmetic also leaves costs from storing and moving data.
missing: A broad demonstration that complete encrypted applications fit ordinary time and memory budgets.
A fair comparison with unencrypted programs, with matching results or clearly stated numerical accuracy.
Complete accounting for setup, keys, data transfer and client work, alongside explicit security assumptions.
Independent reproduction that also exposes workloads where costs become too high.

milestones.explanation: A reproducible suite would have to combine database queries, security calculations and running trained models, with inputs and precision specified. This would demonstrate breadth beyond a system built for one task.

milestones.label: Time and memory stay within tenfold overhead
milestones.explanation: Complete runs would have to keep both elapsed time and peak memory within 10 times unencrypted baselines on the same machine, with matched accuracy. This would test affordability against a meaningful comparison.

milestones.label: Security assumptions and complete costs are explicit
milestones.explanation: The system would have to state its security assumptions and settings, count every processing stage, and explain how shared costs are spread across uses. This would make its practical cost claim assessable.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and reveal limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results with public code and inputs, including larger and longer calculations that exceed the cost threshold. This would establish demonstrated breadth and its limits.

uncertain: The proposed tenfold threshold may suit some application budgets, workload sizes and accuracy needs better than others.
A finite workload suite cannot establish a cost bound for every possible program.
Keeping inputs encrypted does not itself prove server correctness, hide the program or prevent sensitive answers from revealing information.

page.title: Fully homomorphic encryption within tenfold plaintext runtime for CIFAR-10 inference and training
page.definition: Fully homomorphic encryption lets a server evaluate arbitrary circuits on ciphertexts, or encrypted data, without the secret key. The key holder decrypts the output to recover the result. The goal is a programmable accelerator that runs inference and training on DARPA’s seven-layer CIFAR-10 image classifier within ten times the runtime specified for the same computations on unencrypted data. The target concerns these workloads and places no general bound on memory use.

goal.need: Banks need fraud scores in time to act on a transaction. In a small credit-card fraud benchmark, encrypted processing took up to 350 times as long as plaintext processing. With ordinary encryption, even a faster service must decrypt the records to score them. Faster encrypted inference could let a bank obtain a fraud score while keeping both the transaction and the score private from the service, provided the service can return scores on time at the bank’s transaction volume.

statements.body: DARPA, DPRIVE programme manager Tom Rondeau
statements.quote: The goal of DPRIVE is to bring FHE down to the computational speeds we see in plaintext.
Intel plans to design an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) accelerator to reduce the performance overhead currently associated with fully homomorphic encryption.
perform encrypted data computations within a factor of 10 of non-encrypted data computations.
statements.context: The DPRIVE Proposers Day special notice states the programme objective.

completion.title: An FHE accelerator runs DPRIVE CNN inference in ≤25 ms and ten training epochs in ≤10 h.
completion.criterion: A CPU-connected silicon FHE accelerator runs the seven-layer classifier in DARPA’s Figure 7, including its rectified-linear activations, on CIFAR-10. The plaintext baseline uses the same network. Encrypted inference takes ≤25 ms per image and ten encrypted training epochs take ≤10 h. The accelerator runs BGV and supports plaintext moduli 2–1,024, ciphertext moduli 2^15–2^500 and ring dimensions 512–16,384. DARPA favors support for two or three schemes and excludes GPU and FPGA solutions.
completion.set_by: DARPA, DPRIVE solicitation HR001120S0032, Amendment 1, Sections I.C and I.F–H and Figure 7, with per-image and ten-epoch units in the programme metrics chart.
completion.threshold_quote: All proposed solutions must be able to run the BGV FHE scheme.
completion.basis: DARPA sets the final exam. Carnegie Mellon University’s Software Engineering Institute evaluates performer designs on DARPA’s behalf. The runtime limits apply to the two specified computations.

milestones.criterion: Evaluate the scheme’s decryption circuit homomorphically to refresh a ciphertext. The refreshed ciphertext must decrypt to the original message and support further gate evaluation.

goal.need = "Banks need fraud scores in time to act on a transaction. In a small credit-card fraud benchmark, encrypted processing took up to 350 times as long as plaintext processing. With ordinary encryption, even a faster service must decrypt the records to score them. Faster encrypted inference could let a bank obtain a fraud score while keeping both the transaction and the score private from the service, provided the service can return scores on time at the bank\u2019s transaction volume.". Reason: A measured fraud-screening workload explains the cost to users more directly than the survey dates and accelerator count.

add statement by DARPA, Microsystems Technology Office, 2020: "perform encrypted data computations within a factor of 10 of non-encrypted data computations.". Reason: DARPA’s original notice gives the numerical objective that its later public statement describes only as plaintext speed.

edit completion: criterion = "A CPU-connected silicon FHE accelerator runs the seven-layer classifier in DARPA\u2019s Figure 7, including its rectified-linear activations, on CIFAR-10. The plaintext baseline uses the same network. Encrypted inference takes \u226425 ms per image and ten encrypted training epochs take \u226410 h. The accelerator runs BGV and supports plaintext moduli 2\u20131,024, ciphertext moduli 2^15\u20132^500 and ring dimensions 512\u201316,384. DARPA favors support for two or three schemes and excludes GPU and FPGA solutions."; set_by = "DARPA, DPRIVE solicitation HR001120S0032, Amendment 1, Sections I.C and I.F\u2013H and Figure 7, with per-image and ten-epoch units in the programme metrics chart."; threshold_quote = "All proposed solutions must be able to run the BGV FHE scheme."; threshold_ref = 5; basis = "DARPA sets the final exam. Carnegie Mellon University\u2019s Software Engineering Institute evaluates performer designs on DARPA\u2019s behalf. The runtime limits apply to the two specified computations."; refs = [5, 6, 20]. Reason: The solicitation makes BGV mandatory, treats additional schemes as a preference and requires the same specified network for the encrypted and plaintext runs.

edit m1: criterion = "Evaluate the scheme\u2019s decryption circuit homomorphically to refresh a ciphertext. The refreshed ciphertext must decrypt to the original message and support further gate evaluation.". Reason: The bootstrapping criterion mixes the functional test with timings from two implementations that used different parameters.

edit m2: title = "Emulated FHE building blocks execute the 1,024-point logistic regression in under 10 ms."; criterion = "Execute the government\u2019s logistic regression on 1,024 data points using the emulated FHE accelerator building blocks. The application runtime must be less than 10 ms."; set_by = "DARPA, DPRIVE amended solicitation, Section I.C, Phase 1. The Proposers Day chart gives an inclusive limit at 10 ms."; threshold_quote = "1024 data points in less than 10 ms."; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 6, 10]. Reason: Section I.C uses a strict 10 ms limit, and a polynomial-transform cycle count does not measure the regression workload.

add milestone after m1: "Formal verification of the FHE logic blocks reaches at least 90% coverage in under one day.". Reason: Phase 1 has a logic-verification test that a successful regression run alone cannot establish.

add milestone after m2: "The full FHE accelerator emulator executes the 1,024-point logistic regression in ≤1 ms.". Reason: DARPA repeats the regression on the full emulator with a tighter limit than the building-block test.

edit m3: title = "The full FHE accelerator emulator runs CIFAR-10 inference in under 250 ms per image."; criterion = "Execute encrypted inference on the full accelerator emulator using DARPA\u2019s Figure 7 seven-layer network and CIFAR-10. Runtime must be less than 250 ms per image, the Phase 2 target of within 100 times the plaintext runtime on a standard workstation."; set_by = "DARPA, DPRIVE amended solicitation, Section I.C, Phase 2. The Proposers Day chart gives an inclusive limit at 250 ms."; threshold_quote = "in less than 250 ms"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 6, 11]. Reason: Section I.C specifies less than 250 ms, and the criterion currently includes performance projections from particular designs.

add milestone after m3: "Formal verification of the full FHE accelerator reaches 100% logic-block coverage in under one day.". Reason: DARPA requires full logic-verification coverage before fabrication, a separate result from timing the emulated CNN.

edit m4: criterion = "Operate the packaged FHE accelerator on a processing board with the input/output interfaces, firmware and software needed for the host CPU to load data and execute FHE algorithms.". Reason: The board criterion includes a particular chip’s clock speed and bootstrap throughput, neither of which defines board integration.

add milestone after m4: "The FHE accelerator prototype executes the 1,024-point logistic regression in ≤0.1 ms.". Reason: The metrics chart sets a plaintext-speed regression target for the physical prototype that neither emulator test covers.
